newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel presses on with its Jerusalem policies.
newsitem.headline: Israel presses on with its Jerusalem policies.

text.p: Israel felt the blast of international criticism on Wednesday but pressed ahead with its controversial policies in Jerusalem that Arabs say endanger Middle East peace.

A spokesman for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said it would be impossible for Israel to carry out a West Bank pullback due this week in mainly rural areas unless four Palestinian offices in Jerusalem were closed.

"It is impossible for the peace process to continue, for the redeployment and other obligations which Israel has, to continue without the closing of these offices," Netanyahu's media adviser David Bar-Illan told Reuters.

Police backed up the statement by issuing warnings to the four offices, giving them 96 hours to close or face being shut down. It was unclear how the deadline for the closure would affect the Friday due date for Israel's withdrawal.

Arab newspapers identified the four offices concerned as the Palestinian Mapping Office, the Palestinian Small Businesses Project, the Palestinian Institute for the Wounded and the National Islamic Committe Confronting Settlements.
The United States criticised Israel -- for the second time in a week -- calling the decision to shut the four offices "very difficult to understand".

"As the President and the Secretary of State have both said, this is a time when it is very important that the (Middle East) parties take steps that will build confidence between them," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said in Washington.

"It is therefore very difficult to understand why the Israeli government made such a decision at this time when there is a very difficult environment in the relationship with the Palestinians," he told reporters.

In New York, Palestinian President Yasser Arafat told Security Council members that Israel was harming the Middle East peace process by planning a new Jewish neighbourhood on the southern edge of East Jerusalem, captured in the 1967 Middle East war.

Arafat, talking to reporters after meeting with the 15-nation council a few hours before the start of a council debate on israel's plans to build the Jewish settlement, said Netanyahu was ... "pushing the peace process in very critical and crucial circumstances."
The Israeli cabinet's approval last week for the new houses has been criticised by Washington, Arab states and the European Union.
The Palestinians see Arab East Jerusalem as the capital of a future Palestinian state while Israel says Jerusalem will always be its undivided capital.
A visit by Netanyahu to Egypt went ahead as planned, although the Israeli leader arrived in Cairo on Wednesday to hostility from the Egyptian press.
The government newspaper al-Akhbar showed the Israeli leader stuck at a roadblock on the outskirts of Cairo in a limousine. "No Entry", says the road sign.
Netanyahu, on his second visit to the largest Arab state, went straight into talks with Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak.
Afterwards, Mubarak said he was not convinced by Netanyahu's lengthy attempt to justify the decision to build 6,500 homes for Jews in Jerusalem's Jabal Abu Ghneim quarter.
"I cannot tell you I'm convinced. I'm afraid this will create problems in future and I have to look at this again... I'm going to see to it with Mr Arafat, who will be coming tomorrow at night."
German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel said in the Jordanian capital Amman on Wednesday that Israel should reconsider the housing plan.
Kinkel, who met King Hussein on Tuesday night at the start of a trip to Jordan, Israel and Palestinian-ruled Gaza, said he would convey to Israel's government the king's "deep concern".
U.S. President Bill Clinton has said building on the tree-topped Jerusalem hill would fuel mistrust and Arab states have denounced it as a violation of the peace accord with Palestinians.
The PLO's top official in Jerusalem, Faisal al-Husseini, siad the closure orders hard on the heels of the housing plan were a deliberate provocation.
"Although we see that these Israeli measures will cause an explosion we are trying to save matters by contacting the Israelis and other countries to prevent this happening," he told reporters.

"I don't want to hear from the Israelis that they did not know what will happen like they did after the tunnel," he said. "They know, they are certain and they are planning and are heading in that direction consciously and with their full will."

Sixty-one Palestinians and 15 Israeli soldiers were killed in clashes that erupted last September after Netanyahu opened a new entrance to an archaeological tunnel near Moslem holy sites in East Jerusalem.
